title: Alt Text Missing or Empty
desc: Images on the page have no alt attribute, or have alt="" when they convey information. Screen reader users receive no information about the image. Linked images without alt text cause screen readers to announce the URL or file path as the link destination. This is one of the most common accessibility failures and is reliably detected by automated tools.
fix: Add a descriptive alt attribute to every image that carries meaning. The alt value should describe what the image communicates in context, not just what it looks like. For linked images, describe where the link goes or what it does. Set alt="" on images that are purely decorative so screen readers skip them. Do not use file names, "image of", or placeholder text as alt values.
note: This entry covers three common patterns: missing alt on informative images, missing alt on linked images, and alt="" incorrectly applied to informative images. All three fail 1.1.1 for different reasons. Automated tools detect missing and empty alt reliably. Inaccurate alt text requires human review and is covered in a separate entry (ACC-004).

title: Complex Image Has No Sufficient Text Alternative
desc: Charts, graphs, infographics, and diagrams convey information that a short alt attribute cannot fully describe. A brief alt value like "bar chart of monthly revenue" names the image but does not communicate the data, trends, or conclusions it contains. Screen reader users cannot access the information the image is meant to communicate.
fix: Provide a text alternative that conveys the same information as the image. For charts and graphs, an HTML table with the underlying data is usually the most useful alternative. For diagrams and infographics, write a full description in adjacent body text or on a linked page. Use aria-describedby on the image to point to the description. A short alt value is still needed to identify the image; the long description supplements it.
note: A figcaption can serve as the long description when it is thorough enough. Use aria-describedby on the image pointing to the caption element. A caption that only labels the chart type ("Sales by region, 2024") does not satisfy this requirement.

title: Document Is Not Accessible to Screen Readers
desc: A PDF, Word document, or PowerPoint file linked or embedded on the page cannot be read by screen readers. This includes scanned image PDFs with no text layer, documents exported without structure tags, and files where the heading hierarchy and reading order do not match the visual layout. Screen readers either read nothing, read content in the wrong order, or announce raw structural data that does not match the intended meaning.
fix: For PDFs: confirm the file is text-based and tagged. Re-process scanned image PDFs using OCR before tagging. Use Adobe Acrobat Pro to verify and repair the tag tree, reading order, and heading structure. For Word and PowerPoint: use the built-in Heading styles and slide title placeholders rather than manual bold or font-size formatting. Export with document structure tags enabled. If full remediation is not possible, provide an accessible HTML or plain text alternative.
note: This entry covers documents that fail at the foundation level: no text, no tags, or completely wrong structure. More specific failures such as heading structure lost on export or unlabeled PDF form fields are worth noting as separate findings when the document has partial structure but specific gaps.

title: Alt Text Is Inaccurate or Misleading
desc: An image has an alt attribute, but the value does not accurately describe what the image communicates. Common patterns include alt text that describes the visual appearance rather than meaning, file names used as alt values, generic strings such as "image" or "photo", and alt text that misrepresents the data or conclusion an image conveys. This failure cannot be detected by automated tools and requires human review.
fix: Write alt text that answers the question: if this image were removed, what information would be lost? That is the alt value. Do not describe how the image looks; describe what it means in context. Avoid prefixes like "image of" or "photo of". For linked images, describe the link destination. For charts and graphs, summarize the key finding or data, not the chart style.

title: Alt Text Repeats Adjacent Visible Text
desc: An image has alt text that duplicates text immediately adjacent to it, causing screen readers to announce the same content twice in a row. The repeated announcement adds no new information and disrupts the reading flow.
fix: Set alt="" on the image when adjacent visible text already conveys its meaning. The image becomes decorative from the screen reader's perspective, and the visible text does the communicative work. Do not remove the visible text.
note: Severity range: Low to Medium. Lower to Low when it is a single isolated image on an otherwise well-labeled page. Medium applies when the pattern repeats across multiple images or is combined with other redundant label issues on the same page.

title: Decorative Image Announced to Screen Readers
desc: Images used only for decoration or visual spacing are not hidden from assistive technology. Screen readers announce them with file names, image dimensions, or a generic "image" label. Users must listen to these announcements before reaching meaningful content. On native apps, decorative images exposed to VoiceOver or TalkBack produce the same unnecessary interruptions.
fix: Web: mark all decorative images with alt="" so screen readers skip them. CSS background images do not need additional markup. Native iOS: use Image(decorative:) in SwiftUI, or set isAccessibilityElement = false in UIKit. Native Android: set android:contentDescription="@null" and android:importantForAccessibility="no" on decorative ImageView elements. In Jetpack Compose, pass contentDescription = null to Image().
note: This entry covers both web and native app platforms. On the web the fix is alt="". On native apps the fix depends on the framework. In all cases the goal is the same: images that carry no meaning should be invisible to assistive technology.

title: Prerecorded Media Has No Transcript
desc: Audio-only content such as a podcast or recorded announcement, or video content that is not accessible through captions alone, has no text transcript. Deaf and hard-of-hearing users, deafblind users using Braille displays, and users in sound-restricted environments cannot access the content.
fix: Provide a text transcript for all prerecorded audio-only and audio-video content. The transcript must include all spoken dialogue, speaker identification when multiple speakers are present, and meaningful non-speech sounds such as [applause] or [alarm]. Place the transcript on the same page as the media or link to it clearly from the page.

note: This entry covers both audio-only content (which requires a transcript) and video content where a transcript is the chosen alternative to an audio description track. A transcript satisfies SC 1.2.1 for video but does not satisfy SC 1.2.3 or 1.2.5, which require synchronized audio description.

title: Prerecorded Video Has No Captions
desc: A prerecorded video contains spoken dialogue but no synchronized captions are provided. Users who are deaf or hard of hearing, and users watching in sound-restricted environments, cannot follow the spoken content.
fix: Provide synchronized captions for all prerecorded video that contains dialogue or meaningful audio. Captions must be accurate and complete. Auto-generated captions require human review and correction before publishing. A text transcript alone does not satisfy this requirement. Captions must be synchronized with the video.
relatedSC: 1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded) (Level A)

note: Auto-generated captions from platforms like YouTube are a starting point, not a finished product. They must be reviewed and corrected for accuracy, speaker identification, and punctuation before they can be considered compliant.

title: Video Has No Audio Description
desc: A prerecorded video contains important visual information, such as on-screen text, actions, charts, or expressions, that is not conveyed in the audio track. Blind and low-vision users who rely on audio cannot access this visual content. This failure applies at Level A (SC 1.2.3) and again at Level AA (SC 1.2.5), and both are commonly missed together.
fix: Provide a synchronized audio description track that narrates important visual content during pauses in the dialogue. If natural pauses are not long enough, produce an extended audio description version where the video pauses to allow descriptions. A fully descriptive transcript satisfies SC 1.2.3 but does not satisfy SC 1.2.5, which requires the synchronized audio description track. Include both where AA conformance is the target.

note: SC 1.2.3 (Level A) is satisfied by either an audio description track or a full text alternative for the video. SC 1.2.5 (Level AA) requires the audio description track specifically. Both are commonly missed together and worth filing as separate findings.

title: Live Audio or Video Has No Real-Time Captions
desc: A live audio or video broadcast, such as a webinar, live stream, or virtual event, is presented without synchronized real-time captions. Deaf and hard-of-hearing users cannot access the spoken content as it happens.
fix: Provide real-time captions for all live audio and video content. CART (Communication Access Realtime Translation) from a professional stenographer is the most accurate option. Platform-native automatic captions from services like Zoom, Teams, or YouTube Live are acceptable where accuracy is sufficient for the content. Test caption accuracy before the event, not during it.

title: Emoji and Special Characters Disrupt Screen Reader Output
desc: Emoji or special Unicode characters are used in ways that produce verbose or confusing screen reader output. Screen readers announce the full Unicode name of every emoji, so a string of three emoji becomes a string of three lengthy announcements. Special characters used for visual decoration, such as filled circles or directional arrows substituted for common punctuation, produce unexpected announcements in the middle of sentences.
fix: Wrap decorative emoji in a span with aria-hidden="true" so screen readers skip them. For emoji that carry meaning, wrap in a span with role="img" and an aria-label that describes the intended meaning. Limit decorative emoji, especially consecutive ones. Avoid using special Unicode characters in running text where a plain text or HTML equivalent exists. Test with VoiceOver and NVDA to check announcement verbosity.

title: Text Emphasis Relies on Visual Styling Alone
desc: Text that carries meaning through emphasis, such as a warning, key term, or critical instruction, is styled visually with bold or italic CSS but has no corresponding semantic markup. Screen readers do not announce visual styling, so the emphasis is not communicated to screen reader users.
fix: Use semantic HTML to mark up text whose emphasis is meaningful: strong for importance, em for stress. Apply CSS styling on top of the semantic element. If the bold or italic styling is purely decorative and does not change the meaning of the content, CSS alone is acceptable.

title: Landmark Regions Missing, Wrong, or Incomplete
desc: Page sections are not wrapped in landmark regions, use the wrong landmark type, or leave significant content outside any landmark. Screen reader users who navigate by landmark cannot locate the main content, skip past navigation, or orient themselves within the page. Content that falls outside all landmarks is unreachable through landmark navigation shortcuts.
fix: Wrap all visible page content in appropriate landmark regions. Use main for primary content (one per page), nav for navigation link groups, header and footer for page-level regions, aside for supplementary content, and role="search" for search forms. When multiple nav or aside elements exist on the same page, add an aria-label to distinguish them. Do not leave visible content outside landmark containers.

title: Semantic Structure Missing or Incorrect
desc: Content or interactive components use generic elements such as div and span where semantic HTML or ARIA roles should communicate structure. The visual layout implies organization through spacing, color, and position, but none of that structure is available to assistive technology. Screen reader users cannot navigate by structure, and shortcuts for headings, lists, or regions do not apply. This entry also covers composite ARIA widgets whose container is missing required child roles or whose child roles are used outside their required parent, making the widget uninterpretable by screen readers.
fix: Use semantic HTML elements that match the content type: headings for section titles, lists for grouped items, tables for relational data, and button or a for interactive elements. For custom widgets, apply the WAI-ARIA design pattern that matches the intended behavior and implement all required owned and parent roles. Verify the accessibility tree reflects the visual structure using browser DevTools or an accessibility inspector.
note: One of the highest-volume findings in any audit. Missing semantic structure is also a common root cause of apparent 4.1.2 failures, so confirm which SC actually applies before filing both. This entry also absorbs widget role relationship failures, for example a listbox missing its option children, which are too technical to warrant a separate beginner entry.

title: Tabular Data Not Marked Up as a Table
desc: Data arranged in rows and columns is not implemented as an HTML table, or uses table markup without correctly associating header cells to data cells. Screen reader users cannot navigate the table by row and column, and cells are announced without the header context that gives them meaning. A table where sighted users understand a cell value by looking at the row and column headers becomes a sequence of disconnected values for a screen reader user.
fix: Use table, thead, tbody, tr, th, and td to mark up tabular data. Add scope="col" to column headers and scope="row" to row headers. For tables with complex or spanning headers, assign unique id attributes to each th and reference them in headers attributes on the corresponding td cells. Add a caption to identify the table purpose. Do not use CSS grid or flexbox to visually arrange data that has row-and-column relationships.

title: Modal Does Not Hide Background Content from Screen Readers
desc: When a modal dialog is open, background content behind it remains accessible to screen readers. Screen reader users can navigate past the modal into the underlying page, access controls that should be inactive, and lose their position in the dialog. The modal boundary is not communicated to assistive technology.
fix: Apply aria-hidden="true" to the root content container when a modal opens, and remove it when the modal closes. Alternatively, use the inert attribute on the background container, which browsers now support widely. Do not rely on visual overlay alone. On native iOS and Android, the equivalent is to set accessibilityViewIsModal = true on the modal container, which restricts VoiceOver and TalkBack to elements within it.
note: aria-hidden="true" on a parent element hides all descendants from the accessibility tree, including any focusable elements inside. If the modal itself is a child of the container you apply aria-hidden to, the modal will also be hidden. Apply aria-hidden to the background container, not the modal.

title: Related Content Not Grouped for Screen Readers (Native App)
desc: A set of related elements such as an image, title, and description that form a single logical unit are exposed as separate, unrelated accessibility elements. Screen reader users must navigate each sub-element individually, losing the context that makes the group meaningful. On iOS, VoiceOver reads each label or value in sequence without communicating their relationship. On Android, TalkBack announces each view independently.
fix: iOS UIKit: set isAccessibilityElement = true on the container view and set accessibilityLabel to a combined description. Set isAccessibilityElement = false on child elements the container now represents. SwiftUI: use accessibilityElement(children: .combine) on the container. Android: set android:importantForAccessibility="no" on individual child views that should be absorbed, and provide a combined contentDescription on the parent container. In Jetpack Compose, use Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) on the container.

title: Reading Order Does Not Match Visual Layout
desc: The order in which assistive technology reads content does not match the visual order a sighted user would follow. On the web this happens when CSS positioning, flexbox order, or z-index places elements visually in one order while the DOM order differs. On native apps it happens when accessibility element order is not explicitly set and the platform traverses elements in the wrong sequence. The content may be largely understandable despite the wrong order, or it may be actively misleading.
fix: Web: ensure the DOM order matches the visual reading order. Do not rely on CSS to create a logical reading sequence from a disordered DOM. Use flexbox order or CSS grid area only for visual refinement when the DOM order already makes sense in isolation. Native iOS: set accessibilityElements on container views to explicitly define the traversal order. SwiftUI: use accessibilitySortPriority to control VoiceOver order. Native Android: use ViewCompat.setAccessibilityDelegate to define traversal order via setAccessibilityTraversalAfter or setAccessibilityTraversalBefore.
note: Severity range: High to Critical. Defaulted to Critical because the most common instance (wrong column or sequence order) makes content actively misleading. Lower to High when the deviation is minor and the content remains understandable without the correct sequence. This entry covers both web DOM order failures and native app traversal order failures.

title: Instructions Use Sensory Characteristics Only
desc: Instructions or cues tell users to interact with content using only its visual appearance, position, or shape. For example: "click the green button", "see the form on the right", or "use the icon below". Users who cannot see the page cannot follow these instructions because the referenced characteristic is not available to them.
fix: Include a non-sensory identifier alongside any sensory reference. Add a visible text label to the control being referenced so it can be identified by name. For example: "click the Submit button" instead of "click the green button", or "complete the contact form below" instead of "see the form on the right". Instructions should make sense without needing to see, hear, or physically touch the referenced element.
note: This failure is often missed because it does not cause a visible defect. Look for instructions that reference color ("click the red button"), position ("see the icon to the left"), or shape ("use the round button"). Each instance should reference the element by a non-sensory name as well.

title: Interface Locked to One Screen Orientation
desc: The interface forces portrait or landscape orientation and does not adapt when the user rotates their device. Users with mobility impairments who mount their device in a fixed orientation cannot use the interface. Users who simply prefer a different orientation for comfort or legibility are also affected.
fix: Remove any code that locks orientation. Web: do not use the Screen Orientation API to lock orientation unless the content genuinely requires a specific layout to function, such as a video player with a fullscreen mode. Native iOS: do not restrict supported interface orientations in the app settings or individual view controllers unless absolutely necessary. Native Android: do not set android:screenOrientation in the manifest or programmatically unless the feature cannot function otherwise.

title: Personal Data Fields Not Set Up for Autofill
desc: Form fields that collect personal information such as name, email, address, phone number, and payment details are not configured for browser or system autofill. Users with cognitive disabilities, motor impairments, or memory difficulties who rely on autofill to complete forms accurately are required to type each value manually.
fix: Web: add the autocomplete attribute to all personal data fields using the correct token values from the WCAG autocomplete specification, for example autocomplete="given-name", autocomplete="email", autocomplete="street-address". Native iOS: set the textContentType property on UITextField to the appropriate value, for example .emailAddress, .givenName, .postalCode. Native Android: set android:autofillHints on EditText elements using the supported hint values, for example AUTOFILL_HINT_EMAIL_ADDRESS or AUTOFILL_HINT_NAME.
note: This entry covers both web (autocomplete attribute) and native app (textContentType on iOS, autofillHints on Android) implementations. The token values differ by platform but the requirement is the same: the system must be able to identify the type of personal data the field expects.

title: Color Is the Only Way to Understand Content or State
desc: Information, state, or meaning is communicated using color as the only visual difference. Common examples include form validation states shown only in red or green, required fields marked with a colored asterisk where the color is the only indicator, charts where data series are distinguished by color alone, and status indicators that use color without a text label or icon. Users with color vision deficiency and users in high-contrast or monochrome environments cannot perceive the distinction.
fix: Always combine color with a second visual indicator. For validation states, use icons, border styles, or text labels alongside color. For required fields, include a visible text cue such as "(required)" or an asterisk with a legend, not color alone. For charts, use patterns, labels, or shapes in addition to color. For status indicators, include a text label or icon that conveys the state without relying on color.

title: Links in Body Text Are Distinguished by Color Alone
desc: Hyperlinks within body text are not underlined and are distinguished from surrounding text only by color. Users with color vision deficiency may not be able to identify which words are links. CSS resets and design systems commonly remove the default underline from links, creating this failure across entire sites.
fix: Add a non-color visual indicator to links in body text. An underline is the most widely understood convention and requires no explanation. If underlines are removed for design reasons, the link color must have a 3:1 contrast ratio against the surrounding non-link text, and a visible style change such as underline must appear on hover and focus.
note: WCAG 1.4.1 permits removing the underline if the link has a 3:1 contrast ratio against surrounding text and a non-color indicator appears on hover and focus. In practice, verifying the 3:1 ratio against all surrounding text colors on all page backgrounds is difficult, and underline is the simpler, more reliable solution.

title: Audio or Video Plays Automatically on Page Load
desc: Audio or video begins playing when the page loads without the user initiating it. Screen reader users cannot hear their screen reader output over the unexpected audio. Users with cognitive disabilities, attention-related conditions, or audio sensitivity are disrupted. Users in quiet environments are startled or embarrassed.
fix: Do not autoplay audio or video that includes sound. If autoplay is required for a specific reason, mute the media by default and provide a clearly labeled play button. If audio must play automatically, provide a mechanism to pause or stop it within the first three interactive elements on the page so keyboard users can silence it quickly.
relatedSC: 1.4.7 Low or No Background Audio (Level AAA)
note: This failure applies to any audio that plays automatically on page load, including background music, video with audio tracks, and ambient sound loops. It is commonly misapplied only to background music. Video players with autoplay and sound enabled are just as much a failure.

title: All-Caps Text Makes Content Hard to Read
desc: Text is set in all capital letters in source content or via CSS text-transform: uppercase. All-caps text reduces reading speed and comprehension for most readers. For users of some screen readers, all-caps text may be announced letter by letter as an acronym rather than read as a word.
fix: Use CSS text-transform: uppercase for visual all-caps styling so the underlying text remains in mixed case. Do not type content in all capitals in the source. This preserves screen reader pronunciation while maintaining the visual style. Reserve all-caps for short labels or abbreviations where it is the established convention.
note: No WCAG SC directly requires avoiding all-caps, but the readability impact is well-documented and it is a consistent recommendation across accessibility guidance. File as a best practice with a note on the screen reader announcement risk for content typed in all caps.

title: Text Does Not Meet Minimum Contrast Ratio
desc: Text or text images do not have sufficient contrast against their background. The minimum required ratio is 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt or 14pt bold). Low contrast affects users with low vision, users in bright environments, and users on lower-quality displays. This is the most commonly reported WCAG failure across all types of sites.
fix: Use a contrast checker to measure the ratio between text color and its background. Adjust the foreground or background color until the ratio meets or exceeds the minimum. For normal text: 4.5:1. For large text (at least 18pt, or 14pt and bold): 3:1. Do not rely on hover or focus states to provide contrast only on interaction. Test text on all background colors it may appear against, including inside components and over images.
note: Contrast failures also appear in non-text content such as icons, focus indicators, and form field borders, which fall under SC 1.4.11. Confirm which SC applies before filing. Automated tools detect contrast failures reliably but may miss text rendered over gradient or image backgrounds.

title: Text Is Too Small to Read Comfortably
desc: Body text or UI labels are set at a font size below 12px (or equivalent). Very small text is difficult to read for users with low vision, older users, and users on high-density displays. No WCAG success criterion sets a minimum font size, but small text is a consistent usability and accessibility concern.
fix: Set body text at a minimum of 16px (1rem) and avoid using font sizes below 12px for any visible text. Use relative units (rem or em) rather than fixed pixel values so text scales with the user's browser font size settings. Labels, captions, and supporting text may be smaller than body text but should remain legible at the user's default settings.

title: App Does Not Support System Magnification (Native App)
desc: The app interferes with or disables the operating system magnification features. On iOS this includes Display Zoom and Zoom accessibility feature. On Android this includes Magnification gestures and the Accessibility menu magnification button. Users with low vision who rely on these system-level tools to enlarge the screen are unable to use them within the app.
fix: Do not override or disable system magnification. Test the app with iOS Zoom (triple-tap) and Android Magnification enabled and verify that all content can be enlarged and remains usable. Avoid fixed-size layouts that break when zoomed. Ensure touch targets remain reachable and tappable when the display is magnified.

title: User Cannot Zoom or Resize Text in the Browser
desc: The page prevents the user from zooming or resizing text using browser controls. This is caused by user-scalable=no or maximum-scale=1 in the viewport meta tag. Users with low vision who rely on browser zoom to make text readable cannot increase the text size.
fix: Remove user-scalable=no and maximum-scale=1 from the viewport meta tag. A correctly configured viewport tag looks like: meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1". Responsive layouts should be designed to accommodate zoom rather than blocking it.
note: This is a one-line fix with no layout side effects in responsive designs. It is one of the easiest accessibility issues to remediate and one of the most impactful for users with low vision.

title: Text Does Not Resize or Causes Layout Problems
desc: When the user increases the browser font size or system font size, text does not grow, grows but causes content to be clipped or overlapping, or triggers horizontal scrolling in layouts that should reflow. On native apps, text set to fixed sizes ignores the system Dynamic Type or font scale setting, leaving users unable to increase text size system-wide.
fix: Web: use relative units (rem, em, %) for font sizes rather than fixed pixel values. Test layouts at 200% font size (browser setting) and verify text wraps and containers expand rather than clip. Native iOS: use Dynamic Type by calling UIFont.preferredFont(forTextStyle:) and setting adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true. Native Android: use sp units for all text sizes, not dp or px, so the system font scale applies.
note: This entry covers three related failure patterns: text that ignores system font size preferences on the web, text that ignores Dynamic Type on native iOS, and text that ignores the Android font scale setting. All three have the same root cause (fixed size units) and the same user impact.

title: Text Clips or Truncates when System Font Size Is Increased (Native App)
desc: Labels, button titles, and other text elements clip, truncate, or are replaced with an ellipsis when the user increases their system font size. Fixed-height containers do not grow to accommodate larger text. The content becomes unreadable at accessibility font sizes, which are commonly used by people with low vision.
fix: iOS: avoid fixed-height Auto Layout constraints on text-containing views. Use UILabel with adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true and numberOfLines = 0 to allow wrapping. In SwiftUI, avoid .frame(height:) on text views and use .fixedSize(horizontal: false, vertical: true) to allow vertical growth. Android: set android:layout_height to wrap_content on text-bearing views. Do not use maxLines without a visible overflow mechanism. Test at the largest Dynamic Type or Accessibility font size setting on each platform.
note: This failure is distinct from ACC-030, which covers layout-level reflow failures. This entry is specifically about containers that do not grow with their text content, causing the text itself to be cut off rather than the layout to scroll.

title: Text Is Presented as an Image
desc: Text that could be rendered in HTML is instead embedded in an image file. Users who increase font size, change text spacing, or use custom stylesheets receive no benefit because the text is a fixed raster image. Screen readers read only the alt attribute, not the rendered text. Users with low vision who zoom in see pixelated text that degrades in quality.
fix: Replace images of text with actual HTML text styled with CSS. Logos and logotypes are exempt. Text embedded in charts, promotional banners, or infographics should be reproduced as real HTML text in a nearby visible caption or text alternative. SVG text nodes rendered in the DOM are not images of text if the text content is present in the markup.
note: Buttons rendered as images, text embedded in promotional banners, and text in infographics are the most common real-world instances. Logos and brand marks are explicitly exempt. SVG text is not an image of text when the text node is present in the DOM and can be restyled.

title: Page Requires Horizontal Scrolling at 400% Zoom
desc: When the browser is set to 400% zoom (equivalent to a 320 CSS pixel viewport width), the page requires horizontal scrolling to read content. Users with low vision who zoom in to make text larger must scroll horizontally to read each line, which is disorienting and effortful. Two-dimensional scrolling should only be required for content where it is essential to the function, such as data tables, maps, or complex diagrams.
fix: Design layouts to reflow into a single column at 320px viewport width. Use responsive CSS with fluid units, min/max-width constraints, and media queries to ensure content reflows rather than overflows horizontally. Test by setting the browser viewport to 320px wide or by zooming to 400% on a 1280px screen. Content that genuinely requires two-dimensional layout (such as large data tables) is exempt.

title: Interface Does Not Adapt to High Contrast or Forced Colors Mode
desc: The interface does not adapt when the user activates Windows High Contrast Mode or Forced Colors Mode. Custom-styled components lose their visual boundaries, become invisible, or display incorrect colors because hardcoded values override system color adaptations. Custom scrollbars are a common trigger: they become invisible or non-functional in Forced Colors Mode.
fix: Test in Windows High Contrast Mode (both black and white variants) and in Forced Colors Mode via browser DevTools. Avoid hardcoding colors on interactive components. Use CSS system color keywords (ButtonText, LinkText, CanvasText, Highlight) where browser defaults would otherwise be overridden. Use @media (forced-colors: active) to apply targeted overrides where needed. For custom scrollbars: remove the ::-webkit-scrollbar CSS and allow the native OS scrollbar to render, which adapts automatically.
note: Custom scrollbar CSS (scrollbar-color, scrollbar-width: thin, and ::-webkit-scrollbar overrides) is one of the most common triggers for this failure in modern builds. The safest fix is to remove the scrollbar CSS entirely and let the OS render its native scrollbar.

title: Non-Text Content Does Not Meet Contrast Requirements
desc: Visual elements that are not text but are required to understand or use the interface do not have sufficient contrast against their background. This includes focus indicators, icon buttons, form field borders, chart elements, and UI component boundaries. The minimum required ratio is 3:1. Users with low vision cannot perceive or distinguish these elements at low contrast.
fix: Measure contrast for all non-text visual elements that communicate information or indicate an interactive state. Adjust colors until each element meets 3:1 against its adjacent background. Common failures to check: focus rings against the page background, icon-only buttons against their container, input field borders against white backgrounds, and data visualization colors against chart backgrounds.
note: Non-text contrast failures are frequently missed in automated testing. Focus indicators, icon buttons, and input borders are the most common failures. This entry consolidates both the general non-text contrast failure and instances where the issue appears on a specific component type.

title: Text Spacing Cannot Be Overridden or Layout Breaks
desc: The page either uses authored text spacing below the SC 1.4.12 minimums, or the layout breaks when text spacing is overridden to meet those minimums. The minimums are: line height at least 1.5 times the font size, paragraph spacing at least 2 times the font size, letter spacing at least 0.12 times the font size, and word spacing at least 0.16 times the font size. Users with dyslexia or low vision who apply custom spacing through browser extensions or assistive technology cannot read the content when the layout clips or overlaps text.
fix: Ensure containers that hold text can grow with their content. Avoid fixed heights on text containers. Test using the Text Spacing bookmarklet (Steve Faulkner, TPGi) or a browser extension that applies the SC 1.4.12 override values. After applying the override, verify that no text is clipped, no content overlaps, and no functionality is lost. If authored spacing is below the minimums, update the CSS values.
note: The four SC 1.4.12 spacing minimums are: line-height 1.5x font size, paragraph spacing 2x font size, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em. A layout that breaks only when all four are applied simultaneously is still a failure. Test with the bookmarklet before reporting.

title: Tooltip or Hover Content Disappears Too Quickly
desc: Content that appears on hover or focus disappears before the user can read or interact with it. This includes tooltips that vanish when the pointer moves slightly, pop-ups that close on any mouse movement, and hover panels with a timeout shorter than the time needed to read the content. Users with motor impairments who have difficulty maintaining precise pointer position are especially affected.
fix: Content triggered by hover or focus must remain visible until the user dismisses it, moves focus away from the trigger, or moves the pointer off both the trigger and the content. Do not close on pointer movement alone. Do not set a timeout shorter than the time needed to read the content. Allow the pointer to move onto the content itself without the content disappearing.

note: Severity range: High to Critical. Defaulted to High because hover and focus content is frequently supplementary and task completion is usually possible without it. Raise to Critical when the content is the only source of an accessible name, error message, or required instruction.

title: Hover or Focus Content Cannot Be Dismissed
desc: Content that appears when an element is hovered or focused cannot be dismissed without moving focus or the pointer away from the trigger. Users who have increased font size or zoom level may find the content overlaps other content on the page. Users with cognitive disabilities may be distracted by persistent overlapping content they cannot close.
fix: Allow users to dismiss hover or focus content using the Escape key without moving focus or the pointer. This is one of the three SC 1.4.13 requirements alongside persistence and pointer hover. Implement a keydown listener for Escape on the triggering element that hides the content.

title: Escape Key Does Not Close Overlay or Modal
desc: A modal dialog, drawer, dropdown, or other overlay cannot be dismissed by pressing Escape. Keyboard users have no reliable way to close the overlay without navigating to a close button, which may itself be inaccessible. On native apps, the equivalent is a sheet or overlay that cannot be dismissed by a swipe-down gesture or the system back action.
fix: Implement an Escape key listener on modal dialogs and overlays that closes them and returns focus to the trigger element. This is a standard user expectation documented in the WCAG APG dialog pattern. Native iOS: support the swipe-down dismiss gesture on sheets and implement an accessible close button. Native Android: ensure the system Back button dismisses the overlay and that a visible close control is present.
note: Escape key behavior is a WCAG expected behavior and a modal interaction convention. This entry covers both web (Escape key) and native apps (system back gesture and swipe dismiss). It also absorbs the native app overlay dismiss gesture failure.

title: Cookie or Consent Banner Cannot Be Dismissed by Keyboard
desc: A cookie consent banner, GDPR notice, or similar overlay blocks page content and cannot be fully operated by keyboard. The accept, reject, and dismiss controls are not reachable by Tab, cannot be activated by Enter or Space, or are absent from the keyboard focus order. Users who do not use a pointer device cannot dismiss the banner and may be unable to access the content behind it.
fix: Ensure all banner controls are keyboard focusable and activatable. Move focus to the first interactive element within the banner when it appears. If the banner blocks the rest of the page, trap focus within it following the same pattern as a modal dialog. Provide a visible dismiss control that is reachable by keyboard. Do not rely on clicking outside the banner as the only way to close it.
note: Commonly overlooked because the banner is injected by a third-party consent management platform. Keyboard access requirements apply regardless of whether the component is first-party or third-party code.

title: Infinite Scroll Traps Keyboard Users before the Page Footer
desc: A page uses infinite scroll to load additional content as the user scrolls down. The footer and any links or content within it are never reachable by keyboard because new content is continuously inserted before the footer, pushing it further down the page.
fix: Provide a keyboard-accessible alternative to reach footer content. Options include a "Load more" button that replaces automatic loading so users can choose when to load more, a skip link to the footer, or a pagination approach. If infinite scroll is retained, ensure the footer is reachable by Tab and that focus can reach it without requiring the user to scroll through all loaded content.

title: Scrollable Region Is Not Keyboard Accessible
desc: A scrollable container such as a code block, data panel, map, or custom scroll area cannot be scrolled using a keyboard. Users who cannot use a pointer device are unable to access content within the container that is not currently visible. The container receives no keyboard focus and cannot be scrolled with arrow keys or Page Up/Down.
fix: Add tabindex="0" to scrollable containers that contain content not accessible through other keyboard-reachable elements. This makes the container focusable so users can scroll it with arrow keys. Alternatively, ensure all content within the scrollable region is reachable by focusing on elements inside it. Avoid overflow: auto or overflow: scroll on containers whose full content must be accessible without pointer interaction.

title: Non-Interactive Element Receives Keyboard Focus
desc: An element that is not interactive, such as a div, span, paragraph, or image, has been made focusable but performs no action when activated. Users tabbing through the page land on elements that do nothing, which adds navigation steps and causes confusion about what is or is not interactive.
fix: Remove tabindex="0" or tabindex="-1" from elements that are not interactive and serve no navigational purpose. If the element needs to receive programmatic focus (for example, to announce dynamic content), use tabindex="-1" so it can receive focus via script but is not in the tab sequence. If the element is intended to be interactive, add the appropriate semantic role and keyboard event handling.

title: Control Is Not Keyboard Accessible (Native App)
desc: A custom or third-party control in the native app cannot be operated using an external keyboard. Users who connect a Bluetooth keyboard to iOS or Android expect all interactive controls to be reachable and operable. Controls that only respond to touch gestures exclude users who rely on keyboards due to motor impairments.
fix: iOS: ensure all interactive elements are reachable via external keyboard Tab navigation. Custom views must implement UIKeyInput or UIResponder keyboard handling. Test with a connected Bluetooth keyboard. Android: ensure all interactive views respond to Enter key events and are included in the keyboard navigation order. Use ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener and ensure custom views handle KeyEvent.KEYCODE_ENTER.
note: This entry also covers custom controls that are not keyboard accessible on web. Both failures have the same outcome: users who depend on keyboards cannot reach or operate the control.

title: Control Is Invisible until It Receives Keyboard Focus
desc: An interactive control exists in the DOM and is in the keyboard focus order but is not visible until it receives focus. This is sometimes intentional for skip links but is a failure when it applies to any other interactive element. Users navigating by keyboard discover controls they cannot see, and users navigating by pointer do not know the control exists.
fix: Ensure all interactive controls are either always visible or explicitly designed as visible-on-focus elements such as skip links. Skip links must become visible on focus with sufficient contrast. For all other controls, do not use CSS that hides them (opacity: 0, visibility: hidden equivalent) while keeping them focusable. A focusable element that is not visible violates the expectation that the focus indicator is visible.

title: Radio Group Cannot Be Navigated with Arrow Keys
desc: A group of radio buttons does not follow the roving tabindex pattern. Either each radio button is individually in the tab order (requiring multiple Tab presses to move through the group), or the group cannot be navigated using arrow keys at all. The expected keyboard interaction for radio groups is: Tab enters the group, arrow keys move between options, and Tab exits the group.
fix: Implement the roving tabindex pattern for radio groups. Only one radio in the group should be in the tab sequence at a time (tabindex="0"). All others should have tabindex="-1". Use JavaScript to handle arrow key events: ArrowDown and ArrowRight move to the next option, ArrowUp and ArrowLeft move to the previous option. Alternatively, use native HTML input type="radio" elements, which implement this behavior automatically in all browsers.

title: Keyboard Focus Is Trapped inside a Component
desc: Keyboard focus becomes trapped inside a component and cannot be moved out using standard keyboard navigation. The user cannot Tab or Shift-Tab away from the component. This is a critical failure when it occurs in non-modal components such as date pickers, dropdowns, autocomplete widgets, or carousels. Note: a focus trap is intentional and correct behavior inside a modal dialog, where users should not be able to reach background content.
fix: Remove focus trapping logic from any component that is not a modal dialog. Ensure Tab and Shift-Tab cycle through the component and then continue to the rest of the page. For modal dialogs, retain the focus trap but ensure Escape dismisses the dialog and returns focus to the trigger.
note: A focus trap is correct and required inside a modal dialog. It is a critical failure everywhere else. Confirm whether the trapping component is a true modal before filing.

title: Single-Key Shortcut Cannot Be Remapped or Disabled
desc: The interface implements single-character keyboard shortcuts (letters, numbers, or symbols without modifier keys) that cannot be remapped or turned off. Users who navigate by voice or who have motor impairments that cause accidental keypresses activate these shortcuts unintentionally, triggering actions they did not intend.
fix: Provide a mechanism to remap or disable all single-character keyboard shortcuts. At minimum, allow users to require a modifier key (such as Ctrl, Alt, or Meta) to be held with the shortcut key. Single-character shortcuts are only exempt when they are active only on focus of a specific UI component rather than globally.

title: Session Expires without Warning
desc: An authenticated session expires after inactivity with no warning before the timeout occurs. The user is logged out and any unsaved work or form data is lost without any opportunity to extend the session or save progress. Users who take longer to complete tasks due to disability, including screen reader users navigating complex forms, users with motor impairments, and users with cognitive disabilities, are disproportionately affected.
fix: Warn the user before the session expires with enough time to respond. SC 2.2.1 requires at least 20 seconds of warning and a simple mechanism to extend the session, such as pressing a key or activating a button. A modal or status message that appears two to five minutes before expiry and offers an extend option meets this requirement. Sessions that last at least 20 hours satisfy SC 2.2.1 without a warning mechanism.
note: SC 2.2.1 exceptions apply when the timeout is required for security reasons such as in financial or health applications. The warning mechanism requirement still applies even when the timeout itself cannot be removed.

title: Timed Notification Disappears before It Can Be Read
desc: A toast message, snackbar, or timed notification appears briefly and disappears before all users can read it. Users who read slowly, users who are distracted by the visual appearance of the notification, and screen reader users who may not reach the notification before it dismisses all miss the content. If the notification is the only way the information is communicated, those users have no way to retrieve it.
fix: Either set the notification to persist until the user dismisses it, or ensure the information is also available in a persistent location. If a timed notification is used, keep it visible long enough for a slow reader (at minimum 5 seconds per line of text). Place the notification in a live region so screen readers announce it on appearance. Do not auto-dismiss notifications that communicate errors, warnings, or required actions.
note: Toast notifications and snackbars are the most common real-world instance. The notification must persist long enough for a screen reader user to navigate to it, or the content must be placed in a live region that announces it automatically on appearance.

title: Auto-Advancing Carousel Has No Pause or Stop Control
desc: A carousel, hero banner, or slideshow automatically advances through content without user input. No control exists to pause, stop, or hide the moving content. Users with cognitive disabilities and attention-related conditions are distracted by content that changes before they finish reading. Keyboard users cannot keep pace with auto-advancing content.
fix: Provide a visible and keyboard-accessible pause or stop control. Once paused, the carousel must stay paused until the user resumes it. Alternatively, remove auto-advance entirely and let users navigate slides manually. If auto-advance is retained, the interval must be long enough to read all slide content at a comfortable pace.
note: Auto-advancing carousels are widely considered an accessibility and usability anti-pattern. Many experts recommend removing auto-advance entirely rather than providing a pause control as mitigation.

title: Auto-Playing Content Has No Pause or Stop Control
desc: Moving, blinking, or scrolling content that starts automatically and lasts more than five seconds has no mechanism to pause or stop it. This includes animated banners, scrolling news tickers, background videos, and looping animations. Users with cognitive disabilities, attention-related conditions, and vestibular disorders are distracted, disoriented, or unable to use the page while the motion continues.
fix: Provide a pause or stop control for all moving, blinking, or scrolling content that starts automatically and persists beyond five seconds. Place the control in a prominent and keyboard-accessible location. CSS animations triggered only on hover or focus and animations under five seconds are exempt.

title: Flashing Content Exceeds Safe Threshold
desc: Content flashes more than three times per second at sufficient size and contrast. Rapidly flashing content can trigger photosensitive seizures in users with photosensitive epilepsy. This is a safety-critical failure with potential for immediate physical harm.
fix: Remove or redesign any content that flashes more than three times per second. Reduce flash frequency below the threshold, reduce the size of the flashing area, or reduce the contrast of the flash. Test using specialist tooling such as PEAT (Photosensitive Epilepsy Analysis Tool) or HATS. Most automated accessibility testing tools do not detect this failure.
