note: The threshold is three flashes per second at sufficient area and contrast. Most automated tools do not detect this failure. Manual review or specialist tooling (PEAT, HATS) is required.

title: Animations Do Not Respect Reduced Motion Preference
desc: Animations, transitions, parallax effects, and other motion-based interactions play at full intensity regardless of the user's system-level Reduce Motion setting. Users with vestibular disorders, motion sensitivity, or attention-related conditions use this setting to limit motion across their device. Ignoring it exposes those users to motion they have explicitly asked to avoid.
fix: Web: wrap all non-essential animation and transition CSS in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) blocks. Reduce or remove the animation rather than just slowing it. Check JavaScript-driven animations separately because the CSS media query does not automatically suppress animation libraries. Native iOS: check UIAccessibility.isReduceMotionEnabled before starting animations and provide a non-animated alternative. Native Android: check the TRANSITION_ANIMATION_SCALE value or observe AccessibilityManager to detect the reduced motion preference.
note: No WCAG SC at AA requires respecting reduced motion, but it is considered a baseline expectation across expert accessibility guidance. WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA) covers the related concept of animation from interactions. Prefers-reduced-motion is the practical implementation path on the web.

title: Skip Link Is Missing, Not Working, or Not Visible on Focus
desc: The page has no skip link, the skip link does not move focus to the main content area when activated, or the skip link is permanently hidden and never becomes visible on focus. Keyboard users must Tab through every navigation item on every page before reaching the main content. On long navigation menus this can require dozens of Tab presses.
fix: Add a skip link as the first focusable element on every page. The link text should read "Skip to main content" or similar. The link target must be the main content landmark (a element with id or the main element). The link may be visually hidden until it receives focus, but must become visible and meet contrast requirements when focused. Test by pressing Tab on page load and verifying the skip link appears and functions.
note: This entry absorbs three related failures: missing skip link, non-functional skip link target, and skip link that is permanently invisible. All three have the same user impact. A skip link that points to the navigation rather than the main content is also a failure, as users end up where they started.

title: Page Title Is Missing, Non-Unique, or Stale
desc: The page title is absent, generic (such as "Untitled" or the site name only), the same across multiple pages, or does not update when the route changes in a single-page application. Screen reader users hear the page title immediately on load and use it to confirm they have reached the right page. A missing or stale title provides no orientation information.
fix: Set a unique, descriptive title for every page using the title element. The recommended format is "Page Name - Site Name". In single-page applications, update the document title on every route change. Frameworks such as React Router, Next.js, and Angular Router all provide mechanisms to update the document title dynamically.
note: In SPAs, the page title is the first thing announced when a route changes. A static title that never updates means every page announces the same name, giving users no indication that navigation occurred.

title: Focus Order or Focus Management Is Incorrect
desc: The keyboard focus order does not match the visual reading order, focus is not moved to new content when it appears, focus is placed on elements without user initiation, or focus is not returned to the trigger when a dialog closes. These failures cause keyboard and screen reader users to lose their place in the page, encounter content in the wrong sequence, or be surprised by unexpected focus movement.
fix: Ensure the DOM order matches the visual order so Tab sequence is logical. When a modal opens, move focus to the first interactive element inside it. When a modal closes, return focus to the element that triggered it. When content is dynamically inserted or updated, move focus to the new content or to a summary element. Do not move focus to elements the user has not interacted with. Avoid positive tabindex values (tabindex="1", tabindex="2", and so on): they create an unpredictable priority tab ring that overrides natural DOM order and is a common cause of illogical focus sequences. For native apps, use accessibilityElements (iOS) or accessibility traversal order (Android) to define a logical focus sequence.
note: Severity range: High to Critical. Defaulted to High because users can often navigate around unexpected focus order. Raise to Critical when out-of-order focus prevents task completion, for example focus skipping required fields or landing past error messages before the user can correct them. This entry consolidates focus order, focus management after dynamic changes, focus on modal open/close, and focus disruption from dynamic content insertion.

title: Identical Link Text Points to Different Destinations
desc: Multiple links on the page share the same visible text but navigate to different destinations. Users who navigate by link list, which is a common screen reader technique, cannot tell which link goes where. The links are indistinguishable by name alone.
fix: Give each link a unique accessible name that describes its destination. If identical visible labels are required for design reasons, add an aria-label or visually hidden text to differentiate them. For example, "Read more about [Product Name]" rather than "Read more" repeated for each product.

title: Link Text Is Vague, Empty, or Non-Descriptive
desc: Link text does not describe where the link goes or what it does. Common failures include "click here", "read more", "learn more", "details", and "here" used as the entire link text, as well as links with no text content at all. Screen reader users who navigate by link list hear only the link text, without the surrounding paragraph context. A link that reads "click here" in isolation is meaningless.
fix: Write link text that describes the destination or action. For example: "Read the annual report" instead of "click here". If the surrounding context makes the destination clear and cannot be changed, use aria-label or aria-describedby to provide a more descriptive accessible name. Empty links must have an accessible name through aria-label or an img with alt text inside the link.
note: Link text is read in isolation by screen reader users navigating via link list. "Click here", "read more", "learn more", and "details" all fail when used as the entire link text with no additional context provided through ARIA. This entry also absorbs empty link text failures where the link has no accessible name at all.

title: No Alternative Way to Find Pages on the Site
desc: The site provides only one way to find pages, typically navigation menus alone, with no search function, sitemap, or alternative navigation path. Users who have difficulty understanding site structure or navigating menus benefit from multiple ways to locate content.
fix: Provide at least two ways to locate pages. Common approaches include: search functionality, a sitemap page, a table of contents, or related links within content. Single-page sites and pages that are the result of a process step (such as order confirmation) are exempt.

title: Icon-Only Control Has No Visible Text Label
desc: Interactive controls such as buttons, links, and toolbar items display only an icon with no visible text label. Users who are unfamiliar with the icon's meaning, users with cognitive disabilities, and users who magnify the screen to a level where icons become unrecognizable cannot determine the control's purpose.
fix: Add a visible text label to all icon-only controls. If the design cannot accommodate visible text, provide a tooltip that appears on hover and focus, and ensure the control has an accessible name via aria-label that matches the intended action. A visible label is always preferable to a tooltip alone.

title: Heading Structure Is Missing, Incorrect, or Non-Descriptive
desc: The page has no headings, uses headings that skip levels without reason, applies heading markup to non-heading content, or uses headings with generic or empty text. Screen reader users navigate pages primarily by heading. A missing or broken heading structure means users cannot skim to a section, understand the page hierarchy, or jump to content they need.
fix: Use a single h1 for the main page title. Use h2 for major sections, h3 for sub-sections, and so on. Do not skip heading levels to achieve visual styling. Do not use heading elements on content that is not a section title. Heading text must describe the section it introduces. An empty heading element is a failure. A page with no h1 at all is a common instance: screen reader users expect the h1 as the primary entry point when navigating by heading, and its absence forces linear top-to-bottom traversal.
note: This entry absorbs three heading-related failures: missing or incorrect heading structure, heading elements with no text, and non-heading content incorrectly marked as a heading. All three impair heading navigation for screen reader users.

title: Visible Focus Indicator Is Missing or Not Visible
desc: Keyboard-focused elements have no visible focus indicator, or the indicator has been removed with CSS. Users who navigate by keyboard cannot see which element is currently focused. This affects all keyboard users, not only those with disabilities, but is critical for users who rely entirely on keyboard navigation.
fix: Do not suppress the browser default focus indicator with outline: 0 or outline: none in CSS without replacing it with a visible custom style. Provide a focus style that is clearly visible against all backgrounds the element may appear on. WCAG 2.4.11 (Focus Appearance, Level AA in WCAG 2.2) extends this with minimum size and contrast requirements: a 2px perimeter outline with 3:1 contrast against the adjacent background.
note: The most common cause is outline: 0 or outline: none in CSS resets applied without a replacement focus style. This entry covers both web focus indicators and native app external keyboard focus indicators. WCAG 2.4.11 (WCAG 2.2, Level AA) adds minimum size and contrast requirements on top of 2.4.7.

title: Sticky Header or Footer Covers Keyboard-Focused Element
desc: A sticky header, sticky footer, or fixed floating element partially or fully obscures interactive elements when they receive keyboard focus. The focused element is technically in view but hidden behind the fixed element, making it impossible for the user to see which control has focus.
fix: Ensure focused elements are not obscured by fixed or sticky positioned elements. Add scroll-margin-top (or scroll-padding-top on a scroll container) to account for the sticky header height. Alternatively, use the CSS property scroll-padding on the html or scroll container element. Test by Tabbing through all interactive elements while the sticky header is visible and verifying each focused element is fully visible.
note: SC 2.4.12 (Focus Not Obscured Enhanced, Level AAA in WCAG 2.2) requires the focused element to be fully visible. SC 2.4.11 (Level AA) allows partial obscuring. File at AA unless the focused element is completely hidden, in which case 2.4.7 also applies.

title: Multi-Touch Gesture Has No Single-Pointer Alternative
desc: A feature requires a multi-touch gesture such as pinch-to-zoom, two-finger swipe, or a custom multi-finger gesture, and no single-pointer alternative exists. Users with motor impairments who cannot perform multi-touch gestures are unable to access the feature.
fix: Provide a single-pointer alternative for every multi-touch gesture. For pinch-to-zoom: provide zoom in and zoom out buttons. For two-finger scroll: ensure standard single-finger scroll works. For custom gestures: provide buttons or controls that perform the same action. The alternative must be equally accessible and discoverable.

title: Activating a Control Cannot Be Cancelled
desc: A control activates its action on pointer down (mousedown, touchstart) rather than pointer up (click, mouseup, touchend), and no mechanism exists to cancel the action by moving the pointer off the control before releasing. Users who accidentally touch or click a control cannot cancel the action.
fix: Trigger actions on pointer up events (click, mouseup, touchend), not on pointer down. If an action must begin on down (such as a drag operation), provide a mechanism to undo or abort it. Do not use mousedown or touchstart as the sole trigger for actions that cannot be reversed.

title: Accessible Name Does Not Match the Visible Label
desc: An interactive control has a visible text label but the accessible name (the value announced by a screen reader and used by voice control software) is different from or does not start with the visible text. Voice control users who say the visible label to activate the control cannot do so. Screen reader users hear a name that does not match what they see.
fix: Ensure the accessible name of every control either matches the visible label exactly or starts with the visible label text. Accessible names are set by aria-label, aria-labelledby, the label element, or the button content. When using aria-label, it must begin with the same text as the visible label. Do not provide an accessible name that completely replaces the visible label with different wording.
note: This entry covers both web and native app platforms. SC 2.5.3 is specifically about voice control: the accessible name must match or start with the visible label so commands like "click Submit" work. This is distinct from misleading labels (4.1.2) or vague labels (3.3.2).

title: Device Motion Feature Has No UI Alternative
desc: A feature is triggered by device motion such as shaking, tilting, or rotating the device, and no equivalent UI control exists. Users who have mounted their device in a fixed position and users who cannot physically move their device due to motor impairment cannot access the feature.
fix: Provide a UI-based alternative for every device motion feature. For a shake-to-undo gesture: add an undo button. For tilt-to-scroll: ensure standard scroll works. Ensure the motion feature can also be disabled so users who activate it unintentionally can turn it off.

title: Drag-and-Drop Has No Alternative Input Method
desc: A feature requires dragging content from one location to another, and no equivalent single-pointer or keyboard alternative exists. Users with motor impairments who cannot perform dragging movements are unable to use the feature.
fix: Provide a single-pointer or keyboard alternative for all drag-and-drop interactions. For reorderable lists: add move-up and move-down buttons. For drag-to-place interactions: provide a click-to-select and click-to-place alternative. The alternative must be equally functional and discoverable. SC 2.5.7 requires a single-pointer alternative, not necessarily a keyboard one, though providing both is best practice.
note: SC 2.5.7 requires a single-pointer alternative, not necessarily a keyboard alternative. A drag-to-reorder that can also be reordered via a touch-accessible button satisfies the SC even if keyboard is not involved, though keyboard support remains a separate requirement under SC 2.1.1.

title: Touch Target Is Too Small or Overlaps Adjacent Targets
desc: Interactive touch targets are smaller than the 24x24 CSS pixel minimum, or the spacing between adjacent targets is insufficient to prevent accidental activation of a neighboring control. Users with motor impairments, tremors, or large fingers frequently activate the wrong target or miss the target entirely.
fix: Ensure all touch targets meet a minimum size of 24x24 CSS pixels. Where the visible control is smaller, use padding to expand the touch area without changing the visual design. Ensure at least 24px of spacing between the centers of adjacent targets where the targets themselves are smaller than 24px. Test on a physical touch device, not only in a browser simulator. Native apps: use a minimum of 44x44 points on iOS (per Apple HIG) and 48x48 dp on Android (per Material Design). Apply padding or enlarge the touch delegate area where the visible control is smaller than the minimum.
note: This entry covers both targets that are below the 24x24 minimum size and adjacent targets that overlap or are too close together. Both create the same risk of accidental activation. SC 2.5.5 (Level AAA) sets a larger 44x44 minimum.

title: Page Language Attribute Is Missing or Wrong
desc: The html element has no lang attribute, or the lang attribute contains an incorrect language code. Screen readers use the lang attribute to select the correct voice, pronunciation rules, and character set for text-to-speech output. Without it, content may be read in the wrong language with incorrect pronunciation, making it difficult or impossible to understand.
fix: Add a lang attribute to the html element with the correct IETF language tag. For example: lang="en" for English, lang="fr" for French, lang="es" for Spanish. Use the correct subtag for regional variants where needed, for example lang="en-US" or lang="en-GB". An incorrect lang value is as much a failure as a missing one.
note: An incorrect lang value, for example lang="en" on a French page, is as much a failure as a missing one. Both cause mispronunciation. Confirm the attribute value is accurate, not just present.

title: Language of Inline Content Not Specified
desc: A page includes phrases, words, or passages in a language different from the page's primary language, and those passages are not marked with a lang attribute. Screen readers read the foreign-language content using the rules and voice of the primary language, resulting in incorrect pronunciation.
fix: Wrap any passage, phrase, or block of text in a language other than the page's primary language in a span or other element with a lang attribute set to the correct language code. For example, a French phrase on an English page: span lang="fr". Common exceptions: proper names, technical terms, and words in foreign languages that have been adopted into the primary language do not require lang markup.

title: Back Navigation Does Not Return to the Previous Page
desc: The browser back button or the app's back navigation does not return the user to the previous page or view. In single-page applications this commonly happens when route changes are not added to the browser history, causing the back button to exit the application or navigate to the wrong page. Users who rely on back navigation to correct a mistake or retrace their steps are unable to do so.
fix: Ensure all route changes in single-page applications use pushState (or the equivalent router API) to add entries to the browser history. Verify that the back button returns the user to the previous view with the same scroll position and form state. Do not replace the current history entry on navigation unless the transition is intentional (such as a redirect after form submission).

title: Receiving Focus Causes Unexpected Context Change
desc: Moving keyboard focus to an element triggers an automatic action such as submitting a form, opening a new page, or launching a dialog without the user activating the element. Users who Tab through a page to explore its controls experience unexpected navigation or content changes they did not initiate.
fix: Do not trigger actions automatically when an element receives focus. Actions must only occur in response to user activation (click, Enter, Space). Use the focus event only to show visual focus indicators and prepare the element for interaction, not to trigger navigation or content changes.

title: Changing a Form Field Causes Unexpected Navigation or Submission
desc: Selecting a value in a form control such as a dropdown, checkbox, or radio button triggers automatic navigation, form submission, or a significant page change without the user confirming the action. Users who are exploring options or who navigate by keyboard encounter unexpected changes when they do not intend to submit or navigate.
fix: Do not trigger navigation or form submission automatically when a field value changes. Require an explicit action such as clicking a Submit button. If a dropdown must navigate on change for design reasons, add a "Go" button and inform users in advance that selecting an option will navigate the page.
note: This entry also absorbs the specific failure of a form that submits or navigates automatically when a field is completed, which is a common instance of the same SC.

title: No Warning before Opening a New Tab or Window
desc: A link or button opens content in a new browser tab or window without warning the user. Users who do not expect a new tab or window are disoriented, and the browser back button no longer works to return to the previous page. Screen reader users may not notice that a new window has opened.
fix: Warn users when a link will open in a new tab or window. Add text to the link such as "(opens in new tab)" or use an icon with an accessible label. Alternatively, avoid opening new tabs by default and let users decide. If a new window is genuinely necessary, provide the warning in the link's accessible name or adjacent visible text.

title: Navigation Order Is Inconsistent Across Pages
desc: Navigation components that appear on multiple pages present their links in a different order on different pages without reason. Users who learn the navigation layout on one page and rely on that learned pattern to move quickly through the site are confused when the order changes unexpectedly.
fix: Keep the order of navigation links consistent across all pages where the same navigation component appears. Changes to navigation order across pages or sections must be intentional and communicated to the user, not incidental.

title: Controls Are Identified Inconsistently Across Pages
desc: Controls that perform the same function on different pages are labeled or presented inconsistently. For example, a search input labeled "Search" on one page and "Find" on another, or a close button using an X icon on some pages and a text label on others. Users who have learned to identify a control by its label or appearance cannot rely on that knowledge across the site.
fix: Use the same label, icon, and accessible name for controls that perform the same function across all pages. Document control naming conventions in a design system or style guide to ensure consistency across teams.

title: Form Error Is Not Announced or Associated with the Field
desc: When a form is submitted with errors, the error messages are not announced to screen reader users, are not associated with the fields they describe, or are displayed only as a visual change (such as a red border) with no text. Screen reader users complete the submission, receive no feedback, and do not know what went wrong or which field to correct.
fix: After form validation, move focus to a summary of errors at the top of the form, or move focus directly to the first field in error. Associate each error message with its field using aria-describedby. Error messages must be text, not only color or icon. On native apps: announce errors using an accessible live region or by moving VoiceOver or TalkBack focus to the first error field.
note: This entry covers three related failures: errors not announced at all, errors not associated with their fields via aria-describedby, and error state communicated only visually. All three have the same user impact for screen reader users and are often found together in the same form.

title: Form Shows Errors on Field Blur before Submission
desc: Inline validation fires when focus leaves a field, not when the user submits the form. A user tabbing through fields to review them triggers error states on every empty field they pass through, regardless of whether they have attempted to fill them in. The errors are inaccurate at the time they appear and create a confusing and disruptive experience.
fix: Trigger validation on form submission, not on blur. If real-time validation is needed for a specific field such as password match confirmation, apply it only after the user has entered a value and then left the field, not on first blur of a still-empty field. Never flag a field as an error solely because the user moved past it without filling it in.

title: Error Message Does Not Identify the Field or Describe the Problem
desc: Error messages do not tell the user which field caused the error, what went wrong, or both. Generic messages like "An error occurred" or "Please check your entry" give users no actionable information. Users with cognitive disabilities are especially affected, but all users benefit from specific error descriptions.
fix: Write error messages that identify the field by name and describe the specific problem. For example: "Email address is required" or "Phone number must be 10 digits". Avoid generic error messages. If a field has multiple possible errors, describe the specific one that applies.

title: Form Input Is Missing a Label
desc: A form field has no associated label. Screen reader users hear only the field type ("text edit") with no indication of what information to enter. A visible label that is not programmatically associated with its field is also a failure: sighted users can make the visual connection but screen reader users cannot. Placeholder text is not a substitute for a label.
fix: Associate a label with every form field. Use a label element with a for attribute matching the field's id. If a visible label cannot be shown for design reasons, use aria-label or aria-labelledby to provide an accessible name. Native iOS: set the accessibilityLabel on the text field. Native Android: use android:labelFor or android:contentDescription. Never rely on placeholder text as the only label.
note: This entry covers three related failures: no label element present, a label element present but not programmatically associated via for/id, and a checkbox or other control with no visible label. All three leave screen reader users unable to identify the field. Placeholder text is explicitly excluded as it disappears on input and fails contrast in most browsers.

title: Required Field Indicator Is Not Explained
desc: Required fields are indicated by an asterisk or other symbol that is not explained anywhere on the form. Users who are unfamiliar with the convention, users with cognitive disabilities, and screen reader users who cannot see the visual indicator do not know which fields must be completed.
fix: Provide a visible explanation of the required field indicator at the start of the form. For example: "Fields marked with * are required." Mark required fields programmatically using the required attribute or aria-required="true" so screen readers announce the field as required.

title: Form Label Is Too Vague or Misleading
desc: A form field has a label that does not clearly describe what information to enter, uses ambiguous terms, or conflicts with the actual purpose of the field. Examples include a "Name" label on a field that expects a legal full name in a specific format, a "Date" label with no format guidance, and labels that describe the wrong field. Users, particularly those with cognitive disabilities, fill in the wrong information or are unable to determine what is required.
fix: Write labels that clearly and specifically describe the expected input. If a specific format is required, include it in the label or in visible hint text below the field. If multiple fields share similar labels, add context to distinguish them. For example: "First name" and "Last name" instead of two fields both labeled "Name".
note: This entry also absorbs labels that are generic or conflicting, for example two different fields that share an identical label. Both the vague label and the conflicting label failure have the same root problem: the user cannot determine the expected input from the label alone.

title: Placeholder Text Is the Only Label for a Form Field
desc: A form field uses placeholder text as its only label. Placeholder text disappears when the user begins typing, leaving them with no reminder of what to enter. The default contrast of placeholder text in most browsers is insufficient. Screen readers handle placeholder text inconsistently, and some do not announce it as the field label.
fix: Provide a visible, persistent label using the label element for every form field. Use placeholder text only as supplementary hint text, never as the primary label. If the design does not allow a visible label, use aria-label or aria-labelledby.

creditLinks.text: Roselli Do Not Use the Placeholder Attribute

note: Placeholder text fails both persistence (it disappears on input) and contrast (browsers render it below the 4.5:1 minimum by default). It cannot substitute for a label for either reason independently, let alone both.

title: Error Message Does Not Explain How to Fix the Problem
desc: A form validation error message identifies the problem but does not tell the user how to correct it. Users with cognitive disabilities, dyslexia, or limited technical knowledge may understand that an error occurred but not know what change is needed to fix it.
fix: Write error messages that include a suggestion for correction. For example: "Email address is not valid. Enter an address in the format name@example.com." If the field accepts a limited set of values, list the acceptable values. Avoid generic messages like "Invalid input".

title: No Confirmation Step before an Irreversible Action
desc: A form or interface allows the user to trigger an irreversible action such as deleting data, making a purchase, or submitting a legal record, with no opportunity to review, confirm, or cancel. Users who activate the control accidentally or who misread the form cannot undo the action.
fix: Provide at least one of: a confirmation step before the action is executed, a review page that summarizes what will happen, or the ability to reverse the action after it occurs. A confirmation dialog ("Are you sure you want to delete this?") with a clear Cancel option is the most common implementation.

title: Previously Entered Data Is Not Preserved Across Form Steps
desc: In a multi-step form, data entered in earlier steps is not pre-populated when the user goes back to review or correct it. Users must re-enter all previously provided information from memory, which is difficult for users with cognitive disabilities and frustrating for all users.
fix: Preserve user-entered data across all steps of a multi-step form. When the user navigates back to a previous step, pre-fill the fields with the values they previously entered. Maintain form state in component state, session storage, or the equivalent throughout the form session.

title: Authentication Requires a Cognitive Test with No Alternative
desc: The only way to authenticate or complete a security check is by solving a cognitive function test such as a CAPTCHA, a puzzle, or a pattern recognition challenge. Users with cognitive disabilities, memory impairments, or processing difficulties cannot complete these tests reliably. SC 3.3.8 is a WCAG 2.2 requirement.
fix: Provide an alternative to cognitive function tests for authentication. Two-factor authentication via SMS or email, passkeys, or allowing the user to copy and paste a code rather than transcribing it are acceptable alternatives. If a CAPTCHA is used, provide an audio alternative or a non-cognitive alternative method.
note: 3.3.8 specifically prohibits cognitive function tests as the only authentication step without an alternative. Two-factor SMS or passkeys satisfy the SC. This is a WCAG 2.2 requirement and increasingly relevant as CAPTCHA use remains widespread.

title: WebView Content Is Not Accessible to Screen Readers (Native App)
desc: A native app embeds a WebView that displays web content, but the web content inside is not accessible to VoiceOver or TalkBack. Hybrid apps that mix native and web content in a WebView must ensure the web layer meets accessibility requirements just as a standalone web page would.
fix: Ensure the HTML content rendered inside the WebView is accessible: semantic HTML, labels, ARIA roles, and keyboard accessibility all apply. On iOS, WebKit WebViews expose their content to VoiceOver automatically when the HTML is accessible. On Android, WebViews must have JavaScript enabled and the HTML must be accessible for TalkBack to read it. Test with both VoiceOver and TalkBack and verify the WebView content is announced correctly.

title: Custom Widget Does Not Follow the Expected Keyboard Pattern
desc: A custom interactive component such as a combobox, menu, tree, or tablist does not implement the keyboard interaction pattern screen reader users expect. Users who know the standard pattern navigate incorrectly and cannot operate the widget. Custom select widgets that are inaccessible are a common instance of this failure.
fix: Implement the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide pattern for the widget type. Each composite widget type (menu, tree, grid, tablist, combobox, listbox) has documented keyboard interactions. For example, a combobox requires arrow key navigation in the list, Enter to select, and Escape to close. Native HTML equivalents (select, input type="checkbox") implement these patterns automatically and are strongly preferred. ARIA tab patterns (tablist, tab, tabpanel) are a frequent source of this failure: arrow key navigation inside the tab list surprises many users and the pattern is commonly implemented incompletely. If the tabs reveal content panels on the same page, a button-per-panel approach with aria-expanded is often simpler and equally valid.
note: This entry also covers custom select widgets that lack an accessible name and role. A select-style dropdown built from divs without the appropriate listbox or combobox role and keyboard handling is both a role failure and an interaction pattern failure.

title: Incorrect ARIA Role Applied to an Element
desc: An ARIA role is applied to an element that does not match how the element behaves, changing the expectations screen readers create for users. On native apps, an incorrect or missing accessibility role has the same effect: the control is announced as the wrong type, and users apply the wrong interaction model.
fix: Use ARIA roles only when they match the element's actual behavior. A div with role="button" must behave exactly like a button: it must be focusable, it must respond to Enter and Space, and it must have an accessible name. Prefer native HTML elements over ARIA role overrides. If a native element (such as a button or input) is used, do not override its implicit role with role="presentation" or an incorrect role.
note: This entry covers both web (incorrect ARIA role) and native app (incorrect or missing accessibility role) failures. The failure pattern is identical: the announced role does not match the control's behavior, so users cannot operate it using the interaction model for that role.

title: Focusable Element Is Hidden from Assistive Technology
desc: An element is in the keyboard focus order and can receive focus but is hidden from assistive technology using aria-hidden="true". Screen reader users navigating by Tab land on a focused element that their screen reader does not announce, creating a silent focus gap. Users do not know where focus has moved or what the element does.
fix: Never apply aria-hidden="true" to an element that can receive keyboard focus, or to an ancestor of a focusable element. If an element must be hidden from the accessibility tree, also remove it from the focus order by setting tabindex="-1" or making it non-focusable. The aria-hidden attribute is for decorative or redundant content that should not be announced, not for interactive content.
note: aria-hidden="true" on a parent element hides all descendants from the accessibility tree, including any focusable elements inside it. This failure is common when entire sections are hidden with aria-hidden while their interactive children remain focusable.

title: Duplicate ID Breaks Label or ARIA Association
desc: Multiple elements on the page share the same id attribute value. ARIA attributes and label elements that reference IDs (aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, and label for) all resolve to the first matching ID in the DOM. When IDs are duplicated, associations point to the wrong element, silently breaking accessible names and descriptions.
fix: Ensure every id attribute value on the page is unique. Duplicate IDs are reliably detected by automated tools such as axe-core. Avoid generating IDs from repeated template components without ensuring uniqueness. Use JavaScript to generate unique IDs for dynamically created components.
note: The impact is silent: aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, and label for all resolve to the first matching ID in the DOM without error. Automated tools detect duplicate IDs reliably and flag them as critical violations.

title: Dialog or Modal Has No Accessible Name
desc: A dialog or modal has no accessible name. When a screen reader enters a dialog, it announces the dialog role and the dialog's accessible name. Without a name, the user hears only "dialog" with no indication of what the dialog is for. This is especially disorienting when multiple dialogs can appear on the same page.
fix: Add an accessible name to every dialog using aria-labelledby pointing to the dialog's visible heading, or using aria-label if no heading is present. Native iOS: set accessibilityLabel on the modal container or ensure the view controller title is accessible. Native Android: ensure the dialog title is associated with the dialog container.

title: ARIA Menu Roles Applied to Site Navigation
desc: Navigation links are implemented using role="menu" and role="menuitem". These roles are for application-style menus such as a desktop app File menu, not for site navigation. Screen readers announce the structure as a menu and change the expected keyboard behavior: arrow key navigation is expected within a menu, but Tab and Enter are expected for navigation links. Users apply the wrong interaction model and may be unable to navigate the site.
fix: Use nav with a list of anchor elements for site navigation. Remove role="menu" and role="menuitem" from navigation components. If a custom dropdown navigation is needed, it is still a navigation structure, not an application menu, and should use nav, ul, li, and anchor elements with appropriate aria-expanded state on the toggle.
note: role="menu" and role="menuitem" are for application-style menus, not for site navigation. This is one of the most common ARIA misuse patterns. The APG explicitly distinguishes navigation from menu components.

title: Control State Is Not Announced to Screen Readers
desc: An interactive control changes state but the new state is not communicated to assistive technology. Common examples include a toggle button that does not announce pressed or not pressed state, an accordion that does not announce expanded or collapsed, a checkbox that uses a custom icon without aria-checked, and a tab that does not communicate whether it is selected. Screen reader users cannot determine the current state of the control without visual inspection.
fix: Use the correct ARIA state attributes to communicate control state: aria-expanded for collapsible sections, aria-pressed for toggle buttons, aria-checked for checkboxes and toggles, aria-selected for tabs and options. Update these attributes in JavaScript when the state changes. Native HTML elements communicate state automatically when used correctly.
note: This entry also absorbs the failure where aria-disabled or disabled state is not communicated. A control that appears unavailable visually but has no programmatic disabled state is a failure of the same SC.

title: Control Has No Accessible Name, Wrong Role, or Misleading Name
desc: A custom or native interactive element is missing an accessible name, has an accessible name that misidentifies its purpose, or has been assigned a role that conflicts with how it behaves. Screen reader users cannot identify the control, understand its purpose, or predict what it will do when activated.
fix: Every interactive element must have an accessible name, a correct role, and a value that reflects its current state. Accessible names come from visible text content, label elements, aria-label, or aria-labelledby. Roles must match the element's behavior. Names must accurately describe the control's purpose, not its visual appearance. Test with a screen reader to verify the name, role, and value announced for each control.
note: This is the core 4.1.2 catch-all entry. It absorbs: missing accessible name, accessible name that misidentifies the control, and controls with a conflicting role. More specific failures such as duplicate IDs breaking associations (ACC-094) or incorrect ARIA roles (ACC-092) are separate entries.

title: Interactive Elements Are Nested inside Each Other
desc: Interactive elements are nested inside other interactive elements in violation of the HTML specification. Common examples include a button inside an anchor, a link inside a button, or an input inside an anchor. The HTML spec forbids interactive content inside interactive elements. The result is unpredictable behavior across browsers and screen readers: one element may become unreachable, activation may trigger the wrong element, or both elements may fire simultaneously.
fix: Do not nest interactive elements. Place buttons and links adjacent to each other as siblings, not inside one another. If a card or list item needs to be both a link and contain separate action buttons, use the pattern where the card's primary link is a standard anchor and the secondary buttons are siblings positioned over the card using CSS, not nested inside the anchor.

note: Severity range: High to Critical. Defaulted to Critical because the failure is rarely context-dependent. Most instances involve a button inside an anchor or a label wrapping a custom control where the inner or outer element becomes non-functional. Lower to High when both elements remain independently accessible through separate means.

title: Adjustable Control Has No Increment or Decrement Actions (Native App)
desc: A slider, stepper, rating control, or other adjustable element in a native app does not implement the accessibility actions that allow VoiceOver and TalkBack users to increment or decrement the value. Users who interact with the control through assistive technology cannot change its value. The same principle applies to any contextual actions exposed through swipe gestures or long-press menus: if those actions are not mirrored as custom accessibility actions, VoiceOver and TalkBack users lose access to them entirely.
fix: iOS UIKit: implement the UIAccessibilityTraitAdjustable trait and the accessibilityIncrement() and accessibilityDecrement() methods on custom adjustable views. SwiftUI: use the accessibilityAdjustableAction modifier to handle increment and decrement. Android: implement custom AccessibilityNodeInfoCompat actions for increase and decrease on custom adjustable views. For contextual actions available through swipe gestures or long-press menus (delete, reply, archive): iOS: add UIAccessibilityCustomAction objects to the accessibilityCustomActions array of the view, one per action, with a clear name and handler block. Android: override onInitializeAccessibilityNodeInfo and call info.addAction() with AccessibilityNodeInfoCompat.AccessibilityActionCompat for each contextual action.

title: Embedded Frame or iFrame Has No Accessible Name
desc: An iframe element has no title attribute or an empty title. Screen readers announce the frame when focus enters it and use the title to tell users what the frame contains. Without a name, the user hears only "frame" with no context. Unnamed frames are a common finding when third-party widgets, ads, or embedded content are added to a page.
fix: Add a descriptive title attribute to every iframe. The title should describe the frame's content or purpose. For example: title="Twitter timeline widget" or title="Payment processing form". If the frame contains no meaningful content, use title="Empty" or hide it from assistive technology using aria-hidden="true".

title: Hidden or Collapsed Content Is Visible to Screen Readers
desc: Content that is visually hidden by a collapsed accordion, closed menu, or inactive tab is still present in the accessibility tree and reachable by screen reader navigation. Screen reader users encounter content they cannot see and that is not logically part of the current view.
fix: Hide collapsed content from the accessibility tree using display: none, visibility: hidden, the hidden attribute, or aria-hidden="true" on the container. Remove any of these when the content becomes visible. Do not use only opacity: 0 or off-screen positioning to visually hide content, as these do not hide it from screen readers.

title: Unavailable Feature Is Not Marked as Disabled
desc: A control that is currently unavailable, inactive, or not applicable is visually styled to look disabled but is not programmatically marked as disabled. Screen reader users have no way to know the control is unavailable. They may attempt to activate it and receive no feedback, or receive an unexpected error.
fix: Mark unavailable controls using the HTML disabled attribute for native form elements, or aria-disabled="true" for custom controls. aria-disabled is preferred for custom controls where retaining focus is desirable, as it keeps the element in the tab order so users can discover and understand it, while HTML disabled removes it from the tab order entirely. Pair aria-disabled="true" with event handler logic that prevents activation.
note: aria-disabled="true" keeps the element in the tab order, which allows users to discover the control and understand it is unavailable. The HTML disabled attribute removes it from the tab order entirely. For custom controls, aria-disabled is generally preferable.

title: List Elements Are Incorrectly Nested
desc: List markup is structured incorrectly: li elements appear outside ul or ol containers, non-li elements are placed directly inside ul or ol, or lists are nested inside each other in a way that does not reflect the actual content hierarchy. Screen readers announce list structure and item counts. Incorrect nesting produces inaccurate structure announcements.
fix: Ensure all li elements are direct children of ul or ol elements. Only li elements should be direct children of ul or ol. Nested lists must be placed inside an li element, not directly inside the parent ul or ol. Validate list structure using browser DevTools or an HTML validator.

title: Dynamic Content Changes Are Not Announced to Screen Readers
desc: Content that updates dynamically, such as loading states, search results, status messages, countdown timers, and form success or failure messages, is not announced to screen reader users. The visual update occurs silently. Screen reader users receive no indication that anything has changed and must re-navigate the page to discover the new content.
fix: Use ARIA live regions to announce dynamic content changes. Place a live region container in the DOM before the content loads. Use aria-live="polite" for non-urgent updates and role="status" for status messages. For urgent announcements only, use role="alert" or aria-live="assertive". On native apps: use UIAccessibility.post(notification: .announcement) on iOS for important announcements. On Android, use AccessibilityManager.sendAccessibilityEvent() or View.announceForAccessibility().
note: This entry consolidates loading state announcements, expanded content announcements, countdown timer announcements, and general dynamic status updates into one entry. All have the same root cause (no live region) and the same fix (implement aria-live or platform equivalent). Live regions should use aria-live="polite" for routine messages. Reserve role="alert" or aria-live="assertive" for genuinely urgent, time-sensitive notifications.

title: Expanded or Collapsed Content Is Not Announced
desc: When an accordion section expands or collapses, when a disclosure widget reveals or hides content, or when a "Show more" / "Show less" toggle changes the visible content, the change in state and the new content are not communicated to screen readers. Screen reader users activate the control and receive no feedback about what happened.
fix: Add aria-expanded="true/false" to the trigger element (button or heading) and update it in JavaScript when the state changes. Place the collapsible content immediately after the trigger in the DOM so screen readers naturally reach it after the trigger. For content that is inserted rather than shown or hidden, consider a live region announcement that the content has loaded.
